issues.subcategory: SESOI contradictory specification
issues.description: The analytic plan first states the equivalence region is based on a SESOI of δ=.27, but then immediately argues the SESOI should be set to δ=|.11| (matching the smallest observed β from prior literature), calling this 'an extremely conservative analytic decision.' These are two different equivalence bounds (δ=.27 vs δ=.11) within the same paragraph. The study's equivalence tests cannot be pre-registered with two mutually inconsistent bounds, and the discrepancy suggests the text was edited inconsistently. Which bound will actually be used is unclear, and the choice has direct consequences for whether null hypotheses for gambling and substances are supported.
issues.quote: we will use the Anderson-Hauck equivalence test for regression (Counsell & Cribbie, 2015), with an equivalence region based on the smallest effect size of interest (SESOI) of δ= .27. [...] we elected to set our SESOI (δ) for our equivalence interval equal to the observed standardized estimate (β value) corresponding to the smallest effect listed above (β=.11 [...]) [...] Collectively, then, setting our equivalence region to δ= |.11| represents an extremely conservative analytic decision.

issues.subcategory: BPS response scale mismatch between methods and supplemental materials
issues.description: The Methods section describes the Brief Pornography Screen as using 'a three-point scale of 0 (never) to 2 (very often)' with responses summed, implying a maximum sum score of 10. However, the supplemental materials display the actual BPS items with response anchors of Never=0, Occasionally=2, Very Often=4 — a scale that doubles the described values, yielding a maximum sum of 20. The standard validated BPS (Kraus et al., 2020) uses 0/1/2 coding. This discrepancy means the supplemental instrument as operationalized deviates from the validated scale and is inconsistent with the description in the methods, undermining score interpretation, comparison to prior work, and the validity of the outcome variable.
issues.quote: Participants will respond to the prompt, 'In the last 6 months, have any of these situations happened to you in regards to your use of pornography?' by reporting the frequency they have experienced certain behaviors [...] on a three-point scale of 0 (never) to 2 (very often). Responses are summed.

issues.subcategory: PGSI response scale mismatch between methods and supplemental materials
issues.description: The Methods section describes the Problem Gambling Severity Index as using 'a 4-point scale of 0 (never) to 3 (almost always)' — consistent with the standard validated PGSI (Ferris & Wynne, 2001), where summed scores range 0–27 with established clinical cutoffs. The supplemental materials, however, display response options as Never=0, Sometimes=2, Most of the time=4, Almost Always=5. This tripling/non-linear recoding is non-standard, inconsistent with the validated version, and breaks the established severity cutoffs. Additionally, the irregular jump from 4 to 5 (rather than 0→2→4→6) appears to be a further coding error. The methods also say responses 'will be averaged' whereas the validated PGSI sums items, which changes score interpretation and clinical cutpoint applicability.
issues.quote: problem gambling behavior will be measured using the Problem Gambling Severity Index (Ferris & Wynne, 2001). This 9-item measure requires participants to respond to a series of questions [...] on a 4-point scale of 0 (never) to 3 (almost always). Responses will be averaged.

issues.subcategory: Shifting operationalization of moral incongruence within same manuscript
issues.description: The construct of moral incongruence is operationalized differently in different sections of the paper. The introduction consistently and explicitly defines it as 'the interaction of moral disapproval and use [frequency].' The literature review similarly defines it as 'use frequency moderates links between moral disapproval and self-reported feelings of addiction.' However, the Present Study section introduces a completely different operationalization — 'the interaction of moral disapproval of an action with severity of consequences from the action' — which substitutes 'severity of consequences' for 'frequency of use.' These are conceptually distinct constructs. The severity-of-consequences definition would partially overlap with the outcome variable (self-reported addiction symptoms include consequences), introducing tautology. This inconsistency is never resolved and would make the study's construct validity impossible to evaluate.
issues.quote: Central to the proposed study is the measurement of moral incongruence as the interaction of moral disapproval of an action with severity of consequences from the action.

issues.subcategory: Contradictory instructions for centering predictor variables before computing interaction term
issues.description: Within the same Analytic Plan section, two mutually exclusive instructions are given for how the interaction term will be formed. First, the plan states that 'focal predictors (behavioral frequency measures) and moderators (moral disapproval questions) will be centered and their interaction term calculated.' Later, it states that 'key variables will be entered in their raw form during data processing in SPSS, and their product will be computed.' Centering vs. not centering predictors before computing a product term meaningfully affects the interpretation of main effects in moderation analyses (though not the interaction term itself), and this inconsistency would make it impossible to replicate the analytic procedure as described.
issues.quote: focal predictors (behavioral frequency measures) and moderators (moral disapproval questions) will be centered and their interaction term calculated [...] key variables will be entered in their raw form during data processing in SPSS, and their product will be computed.

issues.subcategory: NIDA-ASSIST composite score averages items with non-equivalent response scales
issues.description: The proposed NIDA-ASSIST composite score averages five items that use fundamentally different response scales. Three items use a 0–5 frequency scale (never to more than once per day), while two items (friend/family concern; failure to control) use a 0/3/6 scale. Averaging these directly gives the 0/3/6-scaled items disproportionate weight at extreme scores (max value 6 vs. 5), distorting the composite. Furthermore, the original ASSIST was designed to sum — not average — items, and the specific point-weightings of the 0/3/6 items were calibrated for summation. Averaging violates the instrument's design rationale and produces a composite with no validated reference scores or established cutoffs.
issues.quote: Participants will respond to three frequency based questions [...] on a scale of 0 (never) to 5 (more than once per day) [...] Participants will also respond to two questions [...] for each substance on 3 point scale (0 = No, Never; 3 = Yes, but not in the past 3 months; and 6 = Yes, In the past 3 months). Responses to each of the above five items will be averaged for each substance of interest

issues.subcategory: Cohen's d reported inconsistently for identical effect size
issues.description: The same study (Grubbs, Lee, et al., 2020) and the same effect size values (ΔR²=.012, f²=.016) are cited twice in the analytic plan section with different Cohen's d conversions: first reported as d=.22, then as d=.25. These cannot both be correct. Neither value is mathematically consistent with f²=.016 using standard conversion formulas (f² to d via r: r=√[.016/1.016]=.125; d≈.252), suggesting the first figure (.22) is a rounding or transcription error. This inconsistency undermines the justification for the chosen SESOI.
issues.quote: ΔR2 = .012, f2 = .016, Cohen's d = .22, Grubbs, Lee, et al., 2020 [...] β=.11, ΔR2 = .012, f2 = .016, Cohen's d = .25, Grubbs, Lee, et al., 2020

issues.subcategory: Sports wagering oversample introduces non-comparability across addiction domains
issues.description: The sports wagering oversample (n=1,500) is recruited based on confirmed past-year sports betting behavior, meaning 100% of that subsample engages in gambling. Combined with the representative sample, gambling has an effective N of ~3,325 with highly inflated base rates and a heavily selected subsample. This makes the gambling analysis non-comparable to all other addiction analyses, which rely solely on the representative national sample. Sports bettors who volunteer for such studies may have systematically different moral attitudes toward gambling than the general population (self-selection toward lower moral disapproval), which would directly bias the moral incongruence interaction being tested. The paper treats gambling and other behaviors as parallel domains while using fundamentally different sampling strategies for each.
issues.quote: due to the design of the larger project from which this sample is taken, we will also recruit an additional 1,500 adults with recent (past year) history of wagering on sports generally or sporting events specifically. This will provide us with a total sample of over 4,000 American adults.

issues.subcategory: No pre-registration URL, platform, or registration date specified
issues.description: Despite being titled 'A Registered Report' and claiming a 'pre-registered design' as a key strength in the Limitations section, the manuscript provides no pre-registration URL, no identified repository (e.g., OSF, AsPredicted, ClinicalTrials.gov), no registration number, and no registration date. For a registered report, this information is foundational — without it, readers cannot verify that the hypotheses and analytic plan were committed to before data collection, cannot check for deviations from the registered plan, and cannot distinguish pre-specified from post-hoc decisions. This represents a fundamental reporting failure that undermines the core credibility claim of the registered report format.
issues.quote: Although the proposed work has many strengths (nationally representative sample, pre-registered design, rigorous statistical evaluation of hypotheses)

issues.subcategory: Critically underpowered subgroups for key equivalence tests
issues.description: Table 2 shows that prescription drug misuse (prevalence ~3.5%, projected n=140) has an estimated achieved power of only .301 for detecting the target effect size (f²=.015), and illicit substance use (prevalence 6–12%, projected n=240–480) has power of .472–.764. These are far below the conventional .80 threshold. The paper acknowledges this but the proposed remedy — adjusting the equivalence region to a larger δ — changes the inferential question post-hoc, from 'is this effect null?' to 'is this effect smaller than a prior pornography-context estimate?'. Critically, the paper still reports these as testing the central hypothesis about moral incongruence being absent in substance domains, when in reality these subsamples are too small to provide informative equivalence tests at any clinically meaningful level.
issues.quote: in the case of illicit drug use (prevalence estimated at 6%-12% of the population) and prescription drug misuse (prevalence estimated at 3.5% of the population), it is possible, if not probable, that our final sample sizes will fall below the minimum size required to detect effects that small

issues.subcategory: Gambling frequency: single item administered despite claim of averaging across items
issues.description: The Methods section states that gambling frequency will be measured using 'a single item' but then states 'To form a measure of gambling frequency, an average across gambling behaviors will be taken,' implying multiple items. The supplemental materials confirm only one gambling frequency item exists ('Gambled or placed bets at all'). There is nothing to average. This internal contradiction suggests either an uncorrected draft inconsistency or a planned multi-item measure that was reduced to one item without updating the analytic text. It also means the gambling frequency measure has no reliability estimate possible and is not comparable to the multi-faceted way gambling frequency is typically assessed.
issues.quote: We will assess gambling frequency using a single item. [...] To form a measure of gambling frequency, an average across gambling behaviors will be taken.

issues.subcategory: No multiple comparison correction for primary moderation analyses
issues.description: The paper conducts 8 moderation analyses as primary hypothesis tests and acknowledges multiple outcomes per behavior domain (e.g., both BPS and NIDA-ASSIST items for pornography; both PGSI and NIDA-ASSIST for gambling). Despite this, no correction for multiple comparisons is pre-specified for the primary moderation tests. The paper mentions Holm-adjusted statistics only for bivariate correlations. With 8+ simultaneous moderation tests, the familywise Type I error rate is substantially inflated. This is especially problematic for the key affirmative hypothesis about pornography (H1), where a positive finding among multiple tests is the desired outcome.
issues.quote: Bivariate correlations will be conducted across all included measures and reported using Holm-adjusted test statistics using the psych package. [...] we will conduct 8 moderation analyses for moral disapproval and frequency

issues.subcategory: Multiple contingent equivalence region redefinitions create undisclosed researcher degrees of freedom
issues.description: The paper describes at least three different equivalence bounds that could be applied depending on outcomes: (1) δ=.27 stated initially; (2) δ=|.11| argued subsequently for primary analyses; (3) the lower bound of the 95% CI for the pornography interaction estimate, to be used if underpowered subgroups cannot meet the SESOI. Each redefinition is triggered by a different contingency ('in the event that...', 'should we lack power...'). Because the triggers involve observed data patterns, this constitutes a form of post-hoc flexibility even within a registered report. The paper also notes it will 'adjust analyses accordingly' without fully specifying decision criteria, leaving undisclosed degrees of freedom in the equivalence testing framework.
issues.quote: In the event that, contrary to hypotheses, the effects of moral incongruence for gambling and substances exceed our region of equivalence based on our SESOI, we will conduct exploratory analyses wherein we redefine the region of equivalence using the lower bounds of the 95% CI for the standardized estimate for our pornography outcome.

issues.subcategory: Non-validated extension of NIDA-ASSIST to pornography and gambling
issues.description: The paper explicitly acknowledges that including pornography and gambling in the NIDA-ASSIST is 'not currently validated' for those behaviors, yet proceeds to use these unvalidated NIDA-ASSIST subscales as primary outcome measures alongside the validated BPS and PGSI. This creates a two-tier measurement system where the validity of comparisons across behaviors depends partly on validated instruments and partly on face-valid adaptations with no psychometric evidence. The authors state this 'will not decrement our ability to evaluate our key hypotheses,' but this is an unsubstantiated claim — unvalidated instruments may have poor reliability, floor/ceiling effects, or systematically different psychometric properties across behavioral domains.
issues.quote: We will also include pornography and gambling as response options on the NIDA-ASSIST [...] Although such an approach is not currently validated for gambling or pornography, given the inclusion of other validated scales to assess these outcomes (see below), including them within the NIDA-ASSIST will not decrement our ability to evaluate our key hypotheses.

issues.subcategory: Causal and predictive language applied to cross-sectional interaction effects
issues.description: Throughout the manuscript, the hypotheses and discussion frame moral incongruence as 'predicting' addiction symptoms, 'contributing to' self-perceived problems, and being 'a leading contributor' — language implying temporal precedence. The study design is explicitly cross-sectional ('this sample is cross-sectional, which limits the temporal ordering of variables'), meaning that a significant interaction between moral disapproval and frequency in predicting concurrent self-reported addiction symptoms cannot establish that moral incongruence causes or temporally precedes those symptoms. The alternative — that people rationalize their addiction-like symptoms by developing moral disapproval post-hoc — is equally consistent with the data but never adequately addressed.
issues.quote: we seek to establish whether moral incongruence (defined as the interaction of moral disapproval of a behavior and the frequency of engaging in that behavior) influences self-perceived feelings of addiction [...] This sample is cross-sectional, which limits the temporal ordering of variables.

issues.subcategory: Stated number of moderation analyses (8) inconsistent with listed behaviors (7) and outcomes (9)
issues.description: The analytic plan states 'we will conduct 8 moderation analyses for moral disapproval and frequency.' However, Table 1 and the explicit listing in the analytic plan identify 7 distinct behaviors (alcohol, tobacco/nicotine, cannabis, prescription drugs, illicit drugs, pornography, gambling). Moreover, the text specifies that pornography and gambling each have two outcome measures (validated scale + NIDA-ASSIST items), which would yield 9 analyses if all outcomes are tested. The number '8' matches neither count and is never explained, leaving ambiguity about which outcome measures will serve as primary analyses for pornography and gambling.
issues.quote: In total, we will conduct 8 moderation analyses for moral disapproval and frequency, corresponding to the 8 target behaviors/variables of interest, with pornography and gambling assessed using the validate measures of problematic use (the Brief Pornography Screen and the Problem Gambling Severity Index, respectively).

issues.subcategory: Confirmatory framing creates expectation bias against finding generalizability of moral incongruence
issues.description: The paper explicitly states 'we aim to demonstrate that [...] the role of moral incongruence in predicting feelings of dysregulation is unique to sexual behavior' and frames finding null effects for gambling and substances as hypothesis confirmation. This is a directional confirmatory bias embedded in the registered hypotheses. The paper acknowledges (in the discussion of what it would mean if results disconfirm) that generalizability of moral incongruence would have 'broad implications,' yet this is framed as 'especially unlikely.' The confirmatory framing toward uniqueness of sexual behavior moral incongruence may not be scientifically justified given the Lewczuk et al. (2020) data already demonstrating non-uniqueness for internet and gaming, and given that the current study's hypotheses about direct effects of moral disapproval are predicted to be positive for ALL behaviors including gambling and substances.
issues.quote: Ultimately, we aim to demonstrate that—consistent with the ICD-11 decision to include moral distress as a diagnostic consideration when applying a diagnosis of CSBD—the role moral incongruence in predicting feelings of dysregulation is unique to sexual behavior, in contrast with other addictions.

issues.subcategory: Single-item moral disapproval measures with no reliability estimation possible
issues.description: Moral disapproval for every behavior (pornography, gambling, alcohol, tobacco/nicotine, cannabis, prescription drugs, illicit drugs) is assessed with a single Likert item. Single items preclude reliability estimation (Cronbach's alpha or omega cannot be computed for one item), cannot capture the multidimensional nature of moral attitudes, and are more susceptible to measurement error. This is particularly problematic because moral disapproval is the key moderator in all 8 primary analyses — measurement error in a moderator attenuates interaction effects and makes it harder to detect equivalence, directly affecting the key null hypotheses for gambling and substances. The paper commits to computing Cronbach's alpha and omega for all included measures but this cannot be done for these critical single-item predictors.
issues.quote: Additionally, we will include a series of single-item moral disapproval questions that match previous measures of moral disapproval of pornography. For each substance, we will ask participants to rate their agreement with the following statement 'I believe that using ________ is morally wrong' on a scale of 1 (strongly disagree) to 7 (strongly agree).

issues.subcategory: Unrealistic assumption of zero missing data with no missing data plan
issues.description: The analytic plan states 'we anticipate no unplanned missingness of data' and provides no plan for handling missing data. Even with professional panel data providers like YouGov, item-level missingness, participant dropout, and skip-pattern errors routinely occur in surveys of this length and sensitivity (covering substance use, gambling, pornography, and morality). Sensitive items about pornography use, illicit drug use, and moral disapproval are especially prone to missing responses due to social desirability. Failing to pre-specify a missing data strategy (e.g., multiple imputation, listwise deletion, or sensitivity analyses) means the paper cannot be fully evaluated or replicated.
issues.quote: As this data will be obtained via YouGov Opinion Polling, certain measures of quality control and responsiveness are guaranteed as a part of their data collection process based on their proprietary data collection standards. Accordingly, we do not anticipate having to remove responses from the dataset due to inattentive or invalid response styles or due to careless responding. Additionally, we anticipate no unplanned missingness of data.

issues.subcategory: YouGov quality control standards not described, preventing replication evaluation
issues.description: The paper relies on YouGov's 'proprietary data collection standards' for quality assurance but does not describe what those standards involve (e.g., attention checks, response time thresholds, duplicate IP screening, speeder removal criteria). This means readers cannot evaluate the adequacy of data quality control, and the study cannot be replicated using other data collection methods. Registered reports require sufficient methodological transparency for external reviewers to evaluate whether the planned procedures are adequate — this is not achievable when quality control is explicitly described as proprietary.
issues.quote: certain measures of quality control and responsiveness are guaranteed as a part of their data collection process based on their proprietary data collection standards.

issues.subcategory: Binary gender coding excludes non-binary and transgender participants from analysis
issues.description: The analytic plan specifies that gender will be included as a covariate coded 'binary where 1 = male, and 0 = not-male.' For a nationally representative U.S. sample of 4,000 adults, this coding scheme collapses transgender men, transgender women, non-binary individuals, and cisgender women into a single reference category, losing potentially important variation. Beyond the covariate coding, the NIDA Quick Screen uses gendered alcohol thresholds (4 drinks for women, 5 for men), which is not applicable to non-binary individuals. With an increasingly recognized non-binary population in U.S. representative samples, this binary treatment is both analytically limiting and potentially misaligns with the YouGov panel's gender data collection practices.
issues.quote: Interactions will be tested using this program with gender (binary where 1 = male, and 0 =not-male), age, and overall religiousness included as covariates of the outcome.

issues.subcategory: Gambling findings not generalizable to general population due to oversample design
issues.description: The paper presents results across behaviors as if they are directly comparable for establishing the uniqueness of moral incongruence to sexual behavior. However, the gambling analysis will incorporate a sports wagering oversample recruited via demonstrated past-year gambling behavior. The resulting gambling sample is disproportionately composed of active gamblers (100% of the oversample), which inflates effect sizes for behavior-outcome associations and may systematically alter moral disapproval distributions. Despite Table 2 presenting gambling with its own row as if it is parallel to other behaviors, this non-comparability is not acknowledged in the Limitations section, and the authors plan to draw conclusions about cross-domain uniqueness using non-equivalent sampling designs.
issues.quote: Gambling | 73% (national sample) 100% (sports-betting oversample) | 3,325

issues.subcategory: Undisclosed potential conflict of interest from gambling industry funding
issues.description: The study is explicitly described as funded by the International Center for Responsible Gaming (ICRG), whose stated mission is promoting responsible gambling. Gambling is a central comparison domain in the study, and a key hypothesis is that moral incongruence will NOT predict gambling disorder symptoms — a finding that would minimize the role of personal values in gambling problems, potentially consistent with industry interests in normalizing gambling behavior. No conflict of interest statement is present in the manuscript. For a registered report examining gambling disorder, funder interests are directly relevant to interpretation and should be disclosed.
issues.quote: Participants will be recruited in late March of 2022 as a part of a larger study of sports wagering behaviors in the American populace funded by the International Center for Responsible Gaming.

issues.subcategory: SESOI anchored to pornography-domain prior literature creates circular advantage for primary hypothesis
issues.description: The SESOI for equivalence testing across all behaviors is explicitly derived from effect sizes observed in prior pornography-focused studies (specifically Grubbs, Lee et al., 2020 and Grubbs, Kraus et al., 2020). Using the pornography context to set the bound means that if the pornography interaction is at or above the SESOI, the primary hypothesis is confirmed — but if non-sexual behaviors produce interactions at or above this same porn-derived bound, the null hypothesis is rejected. This creates an analytic asymmetry: the SESOI is calibrated to confirm uniqueness for pornography specifically, not to test whether effects across domains are meaningfully equivalent. An independent, domain-neutral SESOI (e.g., based on minimum clinically important difference in addiction severity scales) would provide a less circular test.
issues.quote: we elected to set our SESOI (δ) for our equivalence interval equal to the observed standardized estimate (β value) corresponding to the smallest effect listed above (β=.11, ΔR2 = .012, f2 = .016, Cohen's d = .25, Grubbs, Lee, et al., 2020). Notably, this effect was observed for an interaction between religiousness (as opposed to moral disapproval directly) and pornography viewing frequency

issues.subcategory: Pornography frequency measure restricted to solitary use, excluding partnered use
issues.description: The pornography viewing frequency item in the supplemental materials asks only about 'Viewed pornography alone (i.e., without a partner).' This operationalization systematically excludes partnered pornography viewing, which is common and may have different associations with moral disapproval and self-perceived addiction. The definition of pornography provided to participants ('any sexually explicit films, video clips or pictures...') does not restrict to solitary viewing, creating a mismatch between the frequency measurement and the broader construct of pornography use for which moral disapproval is assessed. This restriction may undercount overall pornography use, particularly in relationship contexts, and undermines the comparability of the pornography frequency measure with frequency measures used for other substances (which capture all use regardless of social context).
issues.quote: Pornography Viewing Frequency [...] Viewed pornography alone (i.e., without a partner)
